spark.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
spark.summary: Size QPS, storage, memory, and network bandwidth in seconds using powers-of-two byte units and Jeff Dean's latency numbers every engineer should know.
spark.keyTakeaway: When traffic spikes expose hidden coupling, memorize key anchors ($1\text{ day} \approx 86{,}400\text{ s} \approx 10^5\text{ s}$, $1\text{ KB} = 2^{10}$, L1 cache $\approx 1\text{ ns}$, RAM $\approx 100\text{ ns}$, NVMe SSD $\approx 100\text{ }\mu\text{s}$, cross-continent RTT $\approx 150\text{ ms}$) to sanity-check architectures before writing code.
spark.byteSummary:
Size QPS, storage, memory, and network bandwidth in seconds using powers-of-two byte units and Jeff Dean's latency numbers every engineer should know.

In system design interviews and production capacity reviews, a 60-second back-of-the-envelope calculation immediately tells you whether a dataset fits in single-node RAM (Redis), requires SSD-backed sharding.

Memorize key anchors ($1\text{ day} \approx 86{,}400\text{ s} \approx 10^5\text{ s}$, $1\text{ KB} = 2^{10}$, L1 cache $\approx 1\text{ ns}$, RAM $\approx 100\text{ ns}$, NVMe SSD $\approx 100\text{.

concept.whyItMatters: In system design interviews and production capacity reviews, a 60-second [back-of-the-envelope calculation](/concept/capacity-planning-forecasting) immediately tells you whether a dataset fits in single-node RAM (Redis), requires SSD-backed sharding, or saturates a 10 Gbps NIC.
whenToUse: First 5 minutes of any system design interview to establish QPS, peak QPS (2–3x average), 5-year storage, and cache RAM.
Production architecture reviews to verify network egress, IOPS, and memory budgets.
whenNotToUse: Spending 15 minutes doing exact arithmetic in an interview—round aggressively to powers of 10 and powers of 2.
keyPoints: Time shortcuts: $1\text{ day} = 86{,}400\text{ s} \approx 10^5\text{ s}$; $1\text{ month} \approx 2.5 \times 10^6\text{ s}$; $1\text{ year} \approx 3 \times 10^7\text{ s}$.
Latency ladder: L1 cache (~1 ns) < RAM (~100 ns) < 1 Gbps LAN (~500 us) < NVMe SSD random read (~100 us) < HDD seek (~10 ms) < Cross-continent packet (~150 ms).
80-20 rule for caching: caching the hottest 20% of daily traffic in RAM typically serves ~80% of reads.

sections.content:
## Architecture & Trade-Off Matrix

| Operation | Approx. Latency | Relative Scale |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| L1 Cache Reference | ~1 ns | 1x |
| Main Memory (RAM) Reference | ~100 ns | 100x |
| Compress 1 KB with LZ4/Snappy | ~3 us | 3,000x |
| NVMe SSD Random Read (4 KB) | ~100 us | 100,000x |
| Same-AZ / Datacenter Round-Trip | ~500 us (0.5 ms) | 500,000x |
| HDD Seek | ~10 ms | 10,000,000x |
| US West -> Europe Round-Trip | ~150 ms | 150,000,000x |

simulation.title: Back Of The Envelope Estimation — Interactive Execution Walkthrough

steps.title: Normal Request Path
steps.explanation: Caller sends work into the gateway with explicit timeout and concurrency bounds (Normal Request Path).

steps.title: Contention & Load Spike
steps.explanation: The core engine processes the hot path while keeping state transitions deterministic (Contention & Load Spike).

steps.title: Partial Failure Mode
steps.explanation: Under load or replica lag, bounded backoff and isolation prevent cascading saturation (Partial Failure Mode).

steps.title: Convergence & Recovery
steps.explanation: State converges cleanly and telemetry confirms the system returned within its SLO envelope (Convergence & Recovery).

decisionFramework.problem: How to implement Back Of The Envelope Estimation without hitting unbounded tail latency, state divergence, or operational fragility.
decisionFramework.naiveSolution: Use a single unpartitioned path with unbounded retries and synchronous global coordination.
decisionFramework.whyItFails: Global coordination serializes throughput under load, while unbounded retries amplify transient stalls into full outages.
decisionFramework.alternatives: Compare synchronous strict-consistency paths against bounded asynchronous replication, local caching, or partitioned ownership.
decisionFramework.decision: When traffic spikes expose hidden coupling, memorize key anchors ($1\text{ day} \approx 86{,}400\text{ s} \approx 10^5\text{ s}$, $1\text{ KB} = 2^{10}$, L1 cache $\approx 1\text{ ns}$, RAM $\approx 100\text{ ns}$, NVMe SSD $\approx 100\text{ }\mu\text{s}$, cross-continent RTT $\approx 150\text{ ms}$) to sanity-check architectures before writing code.
decisionFramework.tradeOffs: Gains predictable p99 latency and fault isolation in exchange for explicit bounding, observability, and slightly higher implementation complexity.

decisionExercise.prompt: When Back Of The Envelope Estimation experiences a sudden 5x traffic spike alongside a slow downstream dependency, which engineering choice best protects system stability?

options.label: Increase retry counts and remove client timeouts so every request eventually succeeds.
options.explanation: Unbounded retries multiply load on an already struggling dependency and exhaust worker pools.

options.label: Enforce strict latency budgets, bounded jittered retries, and graceful fallback or load shedding.
options.explanation: Bounding retries and isolating slow paths preserves healthy capacity and keeps tail latency predictable.
